Given the extend of the energy transition challenge , cooperation is not just of the essence, it is a moral duty.

With the point of no return rapidly approaching, and stakes this high, momentum must be carried into refined NDCs, improved policies, and swift action.

As individuals, there are many things one can do.
Firstly, staying engaged, and up to date on the latest developments in multiple sectors goes a long way into making informed decisions that could impact generations at a time.

That can be done at the local level through initiatives, at the international level through global networks and UNDP led initiatives.
In addition, sustainably integrating renewable energy technology into nations requires building fair and lasting partnerships across sectors, as well as across nations.

Technology sharing and capacity building efforts can go a long way in this regard.

Although this Academy has equipped you with the knowledge necessary for informed decision-making, your learning does not stop here!
Constant experimentation is key to unlocking new sources of energy and prosperity for society.
The future may be fundamentally different from the present, but it is built today, it may seem distant, but it is just within reach!
The Transformative Horizon of Energy Innovation

The future of energy is fundamentally transformative due to rapid technological advancements, systemic shifts across societal pillars, and groundbreaking innovations in financial and operational models.
This section will explore these dimensions to illustrate how they collectively reshape the global energy landscape.
The accelerating pace of clean energy technology deployment is a cornerstone of the global energy transformation which makes a sustainable energy future increasingly attainable.1
Solar photovoltaic (PV) and wind power are leading the charge
by exhibiting sharp cost reductions and rapid growth in generation capacity, significantly driven by policy support.
Global renewable electricity generation is projected to climb to over 17,000 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2030,
an almost 90% increase from 2023, a volume sufficient to meet the combined power demand of China and the United States.
Solar PV is forecast to become the largest renewable power source globally by 2029, surpassing hydropower, with wind following in 2030

The rapid growth and cost reduction in solar and wind indicate a significant shift in the global power mix.
However, while generation capacity from these variable sources is expanding rapidly, the ability to effectively utilize and distribute this energy is becoming a primary bottleneck.
This means that without equally rapid advancements (and deployment) of energy storage and grid flexibility solutions, the full potential of variable renewables cannot be realized.

This could lead to the curtailment of clean energy.
Investment in storage and grid modernization is a critical enabler for the entire renewable energy transition, transforming intermittent sources into reliable baseload power.
<strong>Innovation is critical for decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors.
Green hydrogen
is identified as a key innovation in the energy sector, requiring advancements in electrolyzer efficiency, integration with renewable energy systems, and safe storage and transport solutions.
Electric vehicles (EVs)
and their associated battery technologies are experiencing rapid growth, driven by years of public investment, private sector competition, and rising consumer demand.
The repurposing of used EV batteries for energy storage within rural microgrids exemplifies a circular economy concept, which reduces waste and creates new jobs.
Green steel

represents a crucial innovation in the industrial sector, requiring breakthroughs in production technologies, with advances in recycling, reuse, and logistics being essential to significantly lower emissions from steel production.
Modern bioenergy
was the largest source of renewable energy globally in 2023, contributing significantly to emissions reductions in transport, buildings, and industry
